name: Cyproterone acetate
lead: Cyproterone acetate (CPA) is a synthetic steroidal antiandrogen and progestin. It blocks androgen receptors and, through its progestogenic action, suppresses gonadotropin release and so lowers testosterone production in men and ovarian androgen output in women.[1][2][15] Because androgens drive oily skin, acne, excess facial and body hair and scalp hair thinning in susceptible women, CPA, usually in a low-dose pill with ethinylestradiol, is prescribed by doctors to clear acne and seborrhoea, reduce unwanted hair growth and slow androgen-related hair loss, which is how it connects to appearance.[1][15]

It is used for palliation in advanced prostate cancer, for hirsutism and severe acne in women, to reduce sexual drive in men with paraphilias, and in hormone therapy for transgender women, where it is widely used in Europe and elsewhere to suppress testosterone while estrogen produces feminising change.[1][15] A Dutch review described spironolactone or cyproterone acetate combined with an oral contraceptive as the safest and most effective approach for hirsutism in women with PCOS or idiopathic hirsutism.[3] Wikipedia describes the combination with an estrogen as one of the most commonly used treatments for hirsutism, and reports improvement of acne in roughly 75 to 90 percent of women on low-dose combined pills or on CPA alone, with symptoms returning in up to 70 percent after stopping.[15]

The European Medicines Agency's 2020 review concluded that meningioma, a rare tumour, rises with dose and cumulative exposure, and tightened conditions for products with 10 mg or more of cyproterone; liver toxicity is a further rare but serious risk.[1][16] CPA has never been marketed in the United States.[15] Community discussion is sparse; mentions on T Nation are brief and mostly relate to hormone and post-isotretinoin threads.[5][6]

paras: CPA is used in advanced prostate cancer as a palliative agent and for reducing hypersexuality or paraphilic behaviour in men [1]. Early trials compared it with other agents in oncology, including a 1989 randomised trial with tamoxifen in pancreatic carcinoma, and a 1990 multicentre trial and review covered clinical applications of antiandrogens [4][7][8].

Wikipedia lists further uses: combined birth control, polycystic ovary syndrome, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, hidradenitis suppurativa, menopausal hormone therapy in combination with estradiol valerate, hot flashes, suppression of the testosterone surge at the start of GnRH-agonist therapy, and precocious puberty, although GnRH agonists have largely replaced it for the last. It is also used in feminising hormone therapy for transgender women.[15] In prostate cancer Wikipedia reports it is less effective than combined androgen blockade and is rarely used today.[15]

In women, CPA is prescribed for hirsutism, severe acne, seborrhea and androgenetic alopecia associated with PCOS or androgen excess, most often at a low dose combined with ethinylestradiol in a 21 on, 7 off regimen [1]. Reviews of androgenetic alopecia describe hormonal investigation in women with signs of hyperandrogenism to direct therapy [9]. A 2003 randomised trial compared treatments for hyperandrogenic alopecia in women, and a 2016 Cochrane review assessed randomised trials of interventions for female pattern hair loss [10][11].

Wikipedia calls CPA combined with an estrogen one of the most commonly used treatments for hirsutism, and lists acne, seborrhoea and scalp hair loss among its dermatological uses in women.[15] Because most cyproterone products are Rx-only and not approved in the US, access depends on the country.[15]

subs.h: Use in hormone therapy for transgender women
paras: Use of CPA in transgender women was reported as early as 1977 and was well established by the early 1990s. In Europe and much of the world it is a common antiandrogen alongside estrogen, whereas spironolactone is the most widely used antiandrogen for transgender women in the United States.[15] Wikipedia reports that estrogen plus CPA suppresses testosterone into the normal female range, while estrogen plus spironolactone generally does not, and that studies found a wide range of CPA doses gave similar testosterone suppression.[15]

The World Professional Association for Transgender Health's Standards of Care, version 8, recommends keeping the CPA dose low to limit fatigue, blood clots, benign brain tumours and liver effects, according to Wikipedia's account.[15] In this context the drug contributes to appearance changes such as reduced body-hair growth and oiliness, which accompany estrogen-driven body changes; a registered cohort study compared coagulation effects of sublingual and oral estradiol with CPA in transgender women.[20]

subs.h: Acne, hirsutism and hair loss in detail
paras: Wikipedia reports that higher cyclic doses added to a pill already containing CPA were no more effective, or only marginally more effective, for severe hirsutism than the pill alone, and that a lower maintenance dose helped prevent relapse. In men with acne, benefits were seen at several doses, but the lower dose was better tolerated and less effective; side effects such as lowered libido and breast changes usually limit male use for skin.[15]

The standard combined pill contains 2 mg CPA with 35 microgram ethinylestradiol and is taken for 21 days followed by a 7-day break. Wikipedia reports that its venous thrombosis risk is similar to pills containing gestodene, desogestrel or drospirenone and roughly 50 to 80 percent higher than pills with levonorgestrel, with an absolute risk of about 1.2 to 9.9 per 10,000 women-years.[22][14]

A 1987 comparative clinical study examined antiandrogens in hirsutism, and the Dutch review recommends CPA or spironolactone with an oral contraceptive for hirsutism [3][12]. For the combined pill, a 2024 randomised trial in overweight women with PCOS compared CPA with ethinylestradiol plus metformin against liraglutide plus metformin over 12 weeks; both improved menstrual cycle and some hormonal and glycaemic measures [13]. Evidence for scalp hair loss specifically rests on the trials and reviews above [10][11].

The 2003 randomised trial in women with hyperandrogenic alopecia compared treatments including CPA, and the Cochrane review of interventions for female pattern hair loss assessed the wider evidence on treatments.[10][11] A registered trial examined ethinyl estradiol with cyproterone acetate in irregular menstruation and hyperandrogenism in 100 women.[19]

A general reference reports a substantially elevated incidence of meningioma, with hazard ratios above 20 for cumulative exposures over 30 grams, and hepatotoxicity, leading regulators to contraindicate it in patients with prior meningioma and to advise avoiding doses above 10 mg daily for extended periods [1]. Combined oral contraceptives are associated with venous thrombosis, and a Cochrane network meta-analysis compared the thrombosis risk across pill types [14].

Wikipedia lists very common effects (10% or more) of CPA as headache, tiredness, reduced libido, erectile dysfunction and lower ejaculate volume in men, and raised liver enzymes; common effects (1 to 10%) include weight change, depressed mood, gynecomastia and breast tenderness. Rare or serious effects include liver toxicity, blood clots, raised prolactin and benign brain tumours, and stopping high doses abruptly can cause adrenal insufficiency.[15]

In 2020 the European Medicines Agency's review concluded that meningioma is rare, occurring in between 1 and 10 in 10,000 people depending on dose and duration, and that most cases followed several years of use at 25 mg a day or more. For products containing 10 mg or more it limited use to androgen-dependent conditions after other options, including lower-dose products, had failed, asked for the lowest effective dose, and required permanent discontinuation in anyone diagnosed with meningioma. For the low-dose 1 or 2 mg combinations with ethinylestradiol or estradiol valerate the data did not show a risk, but as a precaution they were contraindicated in people who have or have had a meningioma. Prostate cancer use was unchanged.[16]
Pharmacovigilance work also followed: a registered study examined what European doctors knew about the safety information for Androcur and other cyproterone acetate treatments.[21]

The EMA first added meningioma to product information in 2009 for doses of 10 mg or more with a contraindication in people with a history of meningioma, and its later review began on 11 July 2019 at France's request. The agency's safety committee issued its recommendation on 13 February 2020, and the coordination group adopted it by consensus in March 2020.[16] Wikipedia also notes that CYP3A4-active drugs and some anticonvulsants can change CPA levels, and that stopping high doses abruptly can cause adrenal insufficiency.[15]

CPA competitively blocks androgen receptors and activates progesterone receptors, which suppresses GnRH pulsatility and reduces LH and FSH; in men testosterone is reduced by up to 70 to 90 percent at standard doses according to a general reference [1]. CPA is classed among 17-alpha-hydroxyprogesterone derivatives in progestin classifications [2]. Its progestogenic effect contributes to ovulation inhibition when combined with ethinylestradiol [1].

Wikipedia gives oral bioavailability of 68 to 100 percent, about 93 percent protein binding to albumin, hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A4 with 15 beta-hydroxycyproterone acetate as the major active metabolite, an elimination half-life of 1.6 to 4.3 days orally, and excretion of roughly 70 percent in faeces and 30 percent in urine.[15]

Wikipedia describes CPA as antiandrogenic, progestogenic and a weak partial glucocorticoid, with a weak inhibitory effect on steroid synthesis and no estrogenic or antimineralocorticoid activity. It is a synthetic pregnane steroid that is an acetylated derivative of 17-alpha-hydroxyprogesterone, with the formula C24H29ClO4.[15] Because it is cleared mainly by CYP3A4, drugs that inhibit or induce that enzyme, such as ketoconazole or rifampicin, can raise or lower its levels.[15]

CPA was first synthesised in 1961 by Rudolf Wiechert at Schering and patented in 1962 as a progestational agent; its antiandrogenic effects were reported in 1965 after an accidental finding in rat fetuses, and it was first used clinically in 1966 for sexual deviance and prostate cancer.[15]

It was marketed as Androcur in Europe in 1973, the first antiandrogen introduced for medical use, entered a birth-control pill with ethinylestradiol (Diane) in 1978, and was approved for prostate cancer in Germany in 1980. It was never introduced in the United States; in Canada Androcur followed in 1987, Androcur Depot in 1990 and Diane-35 in 1998.[15]

Brands include Androcur, Androcur Depot, Cyprostat and Siterone for CPA alone, Diane, Diane-35 and Dianette for the ethinylestradiol combination (co-cyprindiol), and Climen and Femilar for combinations with estradiol valerate.[15][22] The 35 microgram pill (Diane-35) followed the original 50 microgram Diane in 1986.[22]

CPA is sold in almost all developed countries, with the United States and Japan the major exceptions. Wikipedia attributes the US absence to concerns that arose from animal findings with high-dose pregnane progestogens, including breast tumours in beagle dogs, and teratogenicity.[15][22]

On T Nation, CPA appears incidentally: a 2023 poster argued in a discussion of estradiol and libido that one could take CPA to suppress remaining testosterone, and a 2019 thread on post-isotretinoin recovery quotes a review of progestogens with antiandrogenic properties that includes cyproterone acetate.[5][6] In a 2011 thread a poster listed a CPA and ethinylestradiol pill (Diane) among what they had been taking, and a 2008 poster described very low testosterone linked to androgen deprivation therapy with cyproterone acetate.[17][18]

CPA is prescription-only and carries pregnancy category X; it is not approved in the United States.[15] Regulators in Europe tightened conditions for higher-dose products in 2020 after the meningioma review.[16]

Human research includes a 2003 randomised trial in hyperandrogenic alopecia in women, a Cochrane review of female pattern hair loss, a 1987 comparative study in hirsutism, a 2024 PCOS randomised trial and a 1989 randomised trial in pancreatic carcinoma.[7][10][11][12][13] Registered trials include a study of CPA and ethinyl estradiol in irregular menstruation with hyperandrogenism, and a prospective cohort study comparing coagulation effects of sublingual estradiol and oral estradiol with CPA in transgender women.[19][20] No studies of CPA in male pattern hair loss were identified.

lore.intro: CPA is discussed on forums mostly as part of hormone-suppression regimens and recovery threads, and rarely as a cosmetic drug.[5][6][17]

claims.claim: CPA can be added to suppress leftover testosterone.
claims.believers: A 2023 T Nation poster argued that one could take CPA to suppress remaining testosterone during an estradiol experiment.[5]
claims.experts: CPA lowers testosterone by blocking androgen receptors and gonadotropin release; regulators restrict higher doses because of meningioma and liver risks.[1][16]

claims.claim: Antiandrogens like CPA treat acne and unwanted hair.
claims.believers: Prescribers use it, usually as a combined pill, for hormonally driven acne and hirsutism in women, and Wikipedia calls the combination one of the most commonly used treatments for hirsutism.[15]
claims.experts: Reviews list CPA or spironolactone with a pill as effective for hirsutism, with symptoms often returning after stopping.[3][15]

claims.claim: Antiandrogenic progestogens help recovery after isotretinoin side effects.
claims.believers: A 2019 post-isotretinoin thread quotes a review of progestogens with antiandrogenic properties that includes cyproterone acetate.[6]
claims.experts: No published trial in this setting was located; CPA's studied uses are hirsutism, acne and hair loss in women.[10][11]

card.summary: A progestin-antiandrogen used in women for hirsutism, acne and hair loss; effective in the clinic but limited by meningioma and liver risks.
card.note: Dose-dependent meningioma and liver toxicity risk; hair use is in women with hyperandrogenism.

quick.overview:
Cyproterone acetate is a prescription hormone drug that blocks androgens. Doctors use it, often with an estrogen pill, for excess hair growth, severe acne and androgen-related hair loss in women, and for prostate cancer and sexual-drive reduction in men.

Reviews rank it among first-line choices for hirsutism, but it is hardly discussed in looksmaxxing forums.
quick.mechanism: It blocks androgen receptors and acts as a progestin, lowering the brain signals that drive testosterone and estradiol production.
quick.risks: Reported risks include meningioma at higher cumulative doses, liver toxicity, and thrombosis risk when combined with estrogen pills. Regulators restrict long-term high-dose use.

angle.text: For women with androgen-driven acne, hirsutism or hair thinning, CPA addresses the hormonal cause directly. It is prescribed by doctors, usually as a low-dose combined pill.
